COMPLIANCE GAP MEMORANDUM

TO: General Counsel and Board of Directors
FROM: Corporate Governance & Compliance Team
DATE: August 10, 2026
RE: Healthcare Data Privacy Compliance Program — HIPAA Gap Analysis, Deficiency Identification, Risk Assessment, and Remediation Recommendations

I. INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE

This memorandum presents a comprehensive gap analysis of the client's Healthcare Data Privacy Compliance Program (the "Program") under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA), as amended by the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act of 2009, and the implementing regulations at 45 C.F.R. Parts 160 and 164. The analysis reconciles the operative base materials (Matter File 7 — Corporate Governance) against the counterparty's most recent markup of the compliance program agreement, the disclosure schedules and exhibits (including Schedules 3.7 and 5.2 and Exhibit B), and the controlling partner instruction conveyed in the deal team correspondence.

This memorandum identifies (a) deficiencies in the current Program and the counterparty markup, (b) compliance and transactional risks arising from those deficiencies, and (c) remediation recommendations. The analysis addresses each deviation introduced by the counterparty markup and reconciles the parties' respective positions with the controlling instruction priorities.

II. GOVERNING FRAMEWORK AND APPLICABLE REGULATORY STANDARDS

The Program is subject to the following regulatory framework:

A. HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 C.F.R. Part 160 and Subparts A and E of Part 164): Governs the use and disclosure of protected health information (PHI), establishes individual rights (access, amendment, accounting of disclosures), and mandates administrative, physical, and technical safeguards.

B. HIPAA Security Rule (45 C.F.R. Part 164, Subpart C): Requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information (ePHI), including access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, transmission security, and contingency planning.

C. HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 C.F.R. Part 164, Subpart D): Mandates notification obligations to affected individuals, HHS, and, in certain circumstances, the media, within specified timeframes following the discovery of a breach of unsecured PHI.

D. HITECH Act (Pub. L. 111-5): Strengthens HIPAA enforcement, extends certain Privacy and Security Rule protections to business associates, and increases civil monetary penalties.

E. Requirements under the operative Agreement: The base materials describe an agreement containing representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions. These provisions contain compliance commitments that must be reconciled with the HIPAA regulatory framework.

III. CONTROLLING ANALYSIS PRIORITIES

The deal team correspondence conveying the latest partner instruction establishes the following controlling priorities:

(1) The client will concede the counterparty's conversion of the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket.

(2) The client treats any reduction in the survival period for core representations as a walk-away issue (i.e., non-negotiable).

These priorities supersede any earlier communications stating a different ordering and must govern the remediation strategy set forth in this memorandum.

IV. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP DEVIATIONS AND GAP ANALYSIS

The counterparty markup (documented at 100038) accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces the following material deviations from the base materials. Each deviation is analyzed below, reconciled against the applicable schedules and exhibits, and mapped to deficiency and risk assessments.

A. DEVIATION 1: Reduction of Indemnification Cap and Conversion of Basket from Deductible to Tipping

1. Description of Deviation. The counterparty proposes to (i) silently reduce the indemnification cap and (ii) convert the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. Under a deductible basket, the indemnifying party bears losses only after the aggregate loss exceeds the threshold, and only the excess is recoverable. Under a tipping basket, once the aggregate loss exceeds the threshold, the full amount of losses (including those below the threshold) become recoverable.

2. Reconciliation with Base Materials and Schedules. Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. If the indemnification cap is reduced and the basket converted to tipping, the economic allocation of risk for Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities is materially altered in the counterparty's favor. Specifically, a reduced cap limits the seller's/indemnitor's exposure for HIPAA compliance failures and data breach liabilities that are expressly identified as retained liabilities. Schedule 5.2 items must control over general statements in the base materials; accordingly, any markup affecting indemnification must be tested against the retained-liability schedule to determine the quantum of exposure shift.

3. Gap Identification (Deficiency). The Program's indemnification provisions, as revised by the counterparty markup, contain the following deficiencies:
   a. Undefined/Insufficient Cap Calculus: The reduced cap is not calibrated against the expected exposure associated with the scheduled retained liabilities, including regulatory fines, civil monetary penalties under HIPAA (up to $1,919,973 per calendar year for willful neglect), breach notification costs, and third-party claims arising from data incidents.
   b. Failure to Distinguish Compliance Liabilities: The markup does not carve out (or preserve uncapped treatment for) HIPAA compliance liabilities from the general indemnification cap. In market practice, indemnification obligations arising from HIPAA breaches and willful misconduct often carry extended or uncapped liability treatment.
   c. Basket Conversion Risk Allocation: Conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket increases the likelihood and magnitude of recovery for the indemnitee, but combined with the cap reduction, it produces an uneven economic outcome—the indemnitor gains a lower maximum exposure while the indemnitee faces a lower practical recovery threshold. The net effect is a dilution of the compliance accountability that the base materials intended.

4. Risk Assessment. The combined cap reduction and basket conversion create the following risks:
   a. Underinsurance Risk: The reduced cap may be insufficient to cover a material HIPAA breach scenario, leaving the client (as indemnitee) with significant uncovered losses.
   b. Enforcement/Regulatory Risk: If regulatory penalties and remediation costs exceed the reduced cap, the indemnitor may have no economic incentive to maintain robust HIPAA compliance post-closing, increasing future regulatory exposure.
   c. Reputational Risk: A publicly disclosed breach combined with inadequate indemnification coverage could raise shareholder, patient, and regulator concerns about the adequacy of the compliance program's risk allocation structure.

5. Remediation Recommendations.
   a. Per the controlling partner instruction, the client will concede the basket conversion from deductible to tipping. This concession should be documented and accepted in the final agreement. However, the concession should be expressly coupled with confirmation that the basket threshold amount itself remains at the fair-market level set in the base materials, ensuring the tipping effect does not operate to authorize recovery for de minimis claims.
   b. The indemnification cap should be restored to the base materials' level, or, at minimum, renegotiated upward to a level commensurate with the aggregate value of scheduled retained liabilities in Schedule 5.2 plus the reasonable projected cost of HIPAA compliance defense and enforcement matters.
   c. Add a carve-out to the indemnification cap for losses arising from (i) a breach of the HIPAA compliance representations and warranties, (ii) violations of applicable data privacy and security laws due to the indemnitor's willful misconduct or gross negligence, and (iii) regulatory fines and penalties directly attributable to pre-closing conduct that are assessed post-closing.
   d. Ensure that the cap reduction, to the extent any reduction is ultimately agreed, is applied only to general indemnification claims and not to special or compliance-specific indemnities.

B. DEVIATION 2: Material Adverse Effect (MAE) Definition Adds Carve-Outs for Regulatory Action

1. Description of Deviation. The counterparty's markup adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter." The broadened MAE carve-outs would exclude regulatory actions from what constitutes a triggering MAE.

2. Reconciliation with Base Materials and Schedules. Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that directly intersect the markup's MAE carve-outs. The scheduled disclosures confirm that regulatory inquiries are live, material, and known to the parties at signing. The scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. If the MAE carve-outs exclude all regulatory action, then even a materially adverse outcome of one of the two pending inquiries (e.g., a suspension, a significant fine, a cease-and-desist order impacting core operations) would not constitute an MAE. This arrangement would strip the client of its ability to terminate or renegotiate based on regulatory materiality.

3. Gap Identification (Deficiency). The expanded MAE carve-outs present the following deficiencies:
   a. Overbreadth: The carve-out language, as drafted, is not limited to general regulatory changes (e.g., new legislation) but reaches specific investigations, audits, and enforcement actions that are known and pending—materially expanding what would otherwise be a standard exception.
   b. Asymmetry with Schedule 3.7: The carve-outs are inconsistent with the disclosure of two pending regulatory inquiries in Schedule 3.7. The schedules identify these inquiries as material; the markup's carve-outs would undermine the very materiality they disclose.
   c. Failure to Capture MAE Carve-Back: Standard MAE definitions include "carve-backs" (also called "disproportionate effect" provisions) that restore MAE treatment for events that affect the target disproportionately relative to other similarly situated companies. The markup appears to lack such carve-backs for regulatory action affecting the client's healthcare data operations.

4. Risk Assessment.
   a. Transaction Execution Risk: If regulatory action materially degrades the value of the healthcare data compliance operations and does not qualify as an MAE, the client could be compelled to close an impaired transaction.
   b. Inadequate Due Diligence Escalation: The pendency of the two regulatory inquiries (Schedule 3.7) elevates the importance of this deviation. If the carve-outs stand, the client loses the leverage that a properly-scoped MAE definition would provide in negotiating conditions to closing and post-closing remedies.
   c. Regulatory/Compliance Risk: The carve-outs create an incentive misalignment—the counterparty may have reduced impetus to remediate the scheduled inquiries promptly if adverse outcomes are effectively shielded from MAE treatment.

5. Remediation Recommendations.
   a. Narrow the regulatory-action carve-outs to (i) changes in laws or regulations of general applicability enacted after signing and (ii) actions taken by a governmental authority that are not targeted at the Company or its Affiliates as a result of their specific conduct or attributes.
   b. Add a carve-back provision confirming that an MAE shall nonetheless be deemed to occur if the regulatory action has a materially disproportionate effect on the Company relative to other similarly situated companies in the healthcare data sector.
   c. Specifically carve out from the MAE exclusion any adverse outcome, fine, penalty, consent order, or license restriction arising from or related to the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed in Schedule 3.7. The scheduled exceptions must control, and the carve-outs must not operate to negate the materiality of those disclosed inquiries.
   d. Consider drafting a condition precedent to closing that requires the resolution, in a manner not materially adverse, of the pending regulatory inquiries identified in Schedule 3.7.

C. DEVIATION 3: Shortened Survival Period for Core Representations

1. Description of Deviation. The counterparty's markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival of the core representations (including HIPAA compliance representations and warranties).

2. Reconciliation with Base Materials and Schedules. Exhibit B sets forth the survival matrix for representations and warranties. The markup's limitation-period change directly contradicts Exhibit B. Under the base materials, core compliance representations carry extended survival periods consistent with the applicable statutes of limitation for HIPAA enforcement actions. The markup would compress those periods, limiting the client's ability to assert post-closing claims for pre-closing HIPAA noncompliance.

3. Gap Identification (Deficiency). The survival-period reduction presents the following deficiencies:
   a. Conflict with Exhibit B: The survival matrix in Exhibit B establishes the operative survival periods that the markup seeks to supersede. Because the scheduled exceptions control over general statements, and Exhibit B is a controlling schedule, the survival-period reduction must be measured against — and, absent renegotiation, must conform to — Exhibit B.
   b. Statute of Limitations Mismatch: HIPAA enforcement actions by HHS have extended limitations periods. Shortened contractual survival periods would bar private contractual claims before regulators could even complete their investigations, creating a gap between regulatory action and contractual remedy.
   c. Incommensurate with Compliance Representation: HIPAA compliance representations address ongoing obligations, and the counterparty's attempts to shorten survival are inconsistent with standard market practice for compliance representations in healthcare transactions.

4. Risk Assessment.
   a. Walk-Away Issue (as Designated): Per the controlling partner instruction, any reduction in the survival period for core representations is treated as a walk-away issue. This designation elevates the survival-period reduction to a transaction-critical issue. If not resolved in favor of the base materials' survival matrix, the client should be prepared to walk away from the transaction.
   b. Post-Closing Remedial Risk: If the survival period is shortened, the client's ability to recover for misrepresentations discovered after closing—especially HIPAA compliance gaps discovered during post-closing integration audits—would be severely constrained.
   c. Integration Risk: In post-merger integration, HIPAA compliance deficiencies may not surface until months after closing when systems are fully consolidated and access patterns are mapped. A shortened survival period could extinguish claims before these issues are discovered.

5. Remediation Recommendations.
   a. Reject the survival-period reduction for core representations, consistent with the client's walk-away position. Any changes to survival periods must conform to the survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B.
   b. Propose a survival period for core HIPAA compliance representations equal to the longer of (i) the periods set forth in Exhibit B or (ii) the applicable statute of limitations for HIPAA regulatory enforcement plus a reasonable contractual buffer (e.g., one year).
   c. Include a "survival reset" or tolling provision for fraud, willful misconduct, or concealment claims so that such claims remain actionable notwithstanding any agreed survival period.
   d. Document the client's position that any survival-period reduction for core representations is a deal-breaker in the negotiation record to ensure counterparty clarity.

V. ADDITIONAL PROGRAM-LEVEL GAPS, RISKS, AND REMEDIATIONS

Beyond the three markup deviations, the Program should be assessed for baseline HIPAA compliance gaps that the transaction and markup analysis surfaces. The following gaps are identified as areas of concern requiring remediation.

A. SAFEGUARDS AND SECURITY CONTROLS (45 C.F.R. § 164.308–164.312)

1. Deficiency: The Program's administrative, physical, and technical safeguards documentation does not appear to be updated to reflect current security standards, including encryption requirements for data at rest and in transit, multi-factor authentication, and updated access control matrices.

2. Risk: Failure to maintain current safeguards exposes the client to security incidents, HIPAA Security Rule violations, and civil monetary penalties. Under the HITECH Act, penalties for willful neglect can reach $60,626 per violation, up to $1,919,973 per calendar year.

3. Remediation: Conduct a comprehensive HIPAA Security Rule gap assessment, update the Security Management Process, implement periodic risk assessments (at least annually and upon any material system change), and document a corrective action plan for identified deficiencies.

B. BUSINESS ASSOCIATE AGREEMENTS (45 C.F.R. § 164.308(b)(4) and § 164.314)

1. Deficiency: The counterparty markup and schedules do not evidence current, executed business associate agreements (BAAs) with all vendors and contractors that access, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI.

2. Risk: Absence of BAAs exposes the client to vicarious liability for business associate breaches, as well as to HHS enforcement actions for failure to comply with the BAA requirements.

3. Remediation: Inventory all business associates, verify that current executed BAAs are in place (or any required extensions of liability under the HITECH Act are addressed), and include BAA compliance in the closing conditions.

C. BREACH NOTIFICATION PREPAREDNESS (45 C.F.R. Part 164, Subpart D)

1. Deficiency: The Program lacks a documented, tested breach response plan with defined roles, notification templates, and escalation procedures to meet the 60-day individual notification requirement and the 72-hour notification requirement to HHS for breaches involving 500 or more individuals.

2. Risk: Failure to timely notify may result in HHS penalties and reputational damage. Untimely notification for large breaches also triggers mandatory HHS media and press release obligations.

3. Remediation: Develop and test a breach response playbook, pre-draft notification templates, assign a breach response coordinator, and establish contractual breach notification obligations in all BAAs and the operative agreement.

D. ACCESS, AMENDMENT, AND ACCOUNTING RIGHTS

1. Deficiency: The Program does not clearly document processes for responding to individual requests for access, amendment, and accounting of disclosures of PHI within HIPAA-mandated timeframes (30 days for access and amendment, with one 30-day extension; 60 days for accounting of disclosures).

2. Risk: Noncompliance with individual rights provisions exposes the client to enforcement actions and individual or class-action litigation.

3. Remediation: Implement and document processes for tracking, processing, and responding to individual rights requests, including timelines, personnel responsibilities, and escalation procedures. Audit annually for compliance.

E. TRAINING AND WORKFORCE AWARENESS (45 C.F.R. § 164.530(b))

1. Deficiency: The Program does not demonstrate that all workforce members receive HIPAA privacy and security training appropriate to their roles, with documentation of completion, and that training is refreshed when material changes occur.

2. Risk: Untrained workforce members are a leading source of HIPAA violations, including inadvertent disclosures, phishing-related data breaches, and lost or stolen devices.

3. Remediation: Implement a mandatory HIPAA training curriculum for all workforce members, track and document completion, refresh training at least annually and upon material regulatory or program changes, and add role-specific training for personnel handling ePHI in high-risk functions.

F. SANCTIONS AND DISCIPLINARY POLICIES (45 C.F.R. § 164.530(e))

1. Deficiency: The Program does not articulate a consistent, documented sanction policy for workforce members who violate HIPAA policies and procedures.

2. Risk: Absence of a sanctions policy is an express HIPAA Privacy Rule violation (45 C.F.R. § 164.530(e)) and undermines the culture of compliance.

3. Remediation: Adopt a written sanction policy that establishes escalating consequences for HIPAA violations, requires documentation of all sanction actions, and ensures consistent application across all workforce members regardless of seniority.

G. CONTINGENCY PLANNING AND BUSINESS CONTINUITY (45 C.F.R. § 164.308(a)(7))

1. Deficiency: The schedule and exhibit analysis does not reveal a current, tested contingency plan, including a data backup plan, disaster recovery plan, and emergency mode operation plan for maintaining access to ePHI.

2. Risk: Data loss or extended downtime during an emergency creates both operational and regulatory exposure.

3. Remediation: Review, update, and test the contingency plan at least annually; ensure that backup and recovery procedures are validated through documented exercises; and include contingency planning in the post-closing integration checklist.

VI. RECONCILIATION SUMMARY: COUNTERPARTY MARKUP VS. BASE MATERIALS

The following summary table reconciles each counterparty deviation against the base materials, applicable schedules/exhibits, and the controlling partner instruction.

DEVIATION 1 — Indemnification Cap Reduction and Basket Conversion
- Base Material Position: Full indemnification cap per base materials; deductible basket.
- Counterparty Position: Reduced cap; tipping basket.
- Schedule/Exhibit Reference: Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities).
- Controlling Instruction: Client concedes basket conversion.
- Recommended Outcome: Concede tipping basket; restore/adjust cap; add compliance carve-outs.
- Risk Level: Medium (after remediation).

DEVIATION 2 — MAE Carve-Outs for Regulatory Action
- Base Material Position: Standard MAE definition with limited regulatory carve-outs.
- Counterparty Position: Broad carve-outs for regulatory action tied to the matter's issues.
- Schedule/Exhibit Reference: Schedule 3.7 (two pending regulatory inquiries).
- Controlling Instruction: None specific (not addressed by latest partner instruction).
- Recommended Outcome: Narrow carve-outs, add carve-backs, specifically exclude Schedule 3.7 inquiries.
- Risk Level: High (if unresolved).
- Negotiation Status: Open.

DEVIATION 3 — Shortened Survival Period for Core Representations
- Base Material Position: Survival matrix per Exhibit B.
- Counterparty Position: Shortened survival for core representations.
- Schedule/Exhibit Reference: Exhibit B (survival matrix).
- Controlling Instruction: Survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue for the client.
- Recommended Outcome: Reject any reduction to core representation survival; conform to Exhibit B.
- Risk Level: Critical (deal-breaker).
- Negotiation Status: Walk-away if not resolved in favor of Exhibit B.

VII. ACTION ITEMS AND PRIORITY REMEDIATION ROADMAP

The following prioritized action items should be implemented in the order indicated:

PRIORITY 1 — Transactional (Immediate, Pre-Closing)
1. Reject the survival-period reduction for core representations and demand conformance with Exhibit B. Treat as walk-away if not resolved (Per partner instruction).
2. Narrow the MAE regulatory carve-outs and add carve-backs; specifically protect Schedule 3.7 pending inquiries from MAE exclusion.
3. Concede the basket conversion (deductible to tipping) per partner instruction, but confirm the basket threshold remains unchanged and add compliance-specific indemnification carve-outs to the cap.
4. Confirm that Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities are fully protected under whatever final indemnification terms are agreed.

PRIORITY 2 — Program Compliance (Post-Signing, Pre-Closing)
5. Complete HIPAA Security Rule gap assessment and implement corrective actions.
6. Inventory and execute all required business associate agreements.
7. Update breach notification procedures and test the breach response plan.
8. Verify training completion records and update sanctions policies.

PRIORITY 3 — Post-Closing Integration
9. Integrate contingency planning and disaster recovery readiness into the post-closing IT integration plan.
10. Align access controls and audit logging across the combined entity within the first 90 days post-closing.
11. Conduct a post-closing HIPAA compliance audit within the first 120 days to confirm all representations remain accurate and to identify any new compliance gaps.

VIII. CONCLUSION

The client's Healthcare Data Privacy Compliance Program requires remediation on multiple fronts. Three specific deviations in the counterparty markup must be reconciled: the indemnification cap reduction and basket conversion, the MAE carve-outs for regulatory action, and the survival-period reduction. Of these, the survival-period reduction is the highest-priority issue and, per the controlling partner instruction, constitutes a walk-away issue if not resolved in the client's favor. The others, while material, are either concedable (basket conversion) or negotiable with appropriate narrowing and carve-backs (MAE carve-outs and cap).

In addition to the transactional deviations, this memo identifies baseline HIPAA compliance gaps in the Program—including safeguards updates, BAA coverage, breach notification preparedness, individual rights processes, workforce training, sanctions policies, and contingency planning—that should be remediated through the prioritized roadmap set forth above.

The misfiled administrative correspondence located in the matter folder was reviewed only to confirm it is inapplicable and has been excluded from all analysis in this memorandum.

The firm recommends that the corporate governance team proceed with the transactional remediation items immediately, and that the compliance team simultaneously begin work on the program-level remediation roadmap to ensure the client's HIPAA compliance posture is transaction-ready.

[END OF MEMORANDUM]
